name: BST Construction / Insertion-Order Simulation
recognitionClueHinglish: Numbers ki ek sequence di hai jo empty BST me INSERT honi hai (given order me), aur poocha hai resulting tree ka structure/height/traversal/subtree-size kya hoga — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (36 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Insert one number at a time: compare with current node, go left if smaller, right if larger, repeat until you hit an empty spot.
Draw the tree explicitly after EACH insertion — don't try to build it all in your head.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. For each number in the given order, walk from root comparing and moving left/right until finding an empty position, insert there.
3. Once fully built, answer whatever is asked (height, subtree sizes, traversal, specific node's position).
variationsObserved: Combined with array/heap representation (BST that also happens to be a complete binary tree, stored in array form).
'How many insertion ORDERS produce a specific resulting shape/height' — combinatorial counting on top of simulation.
commonTraps: Losing track of which subtree a number belongs to partway through a long insertion sequence — always re-draw rather than trust memory.
edgeCases: Sorted or reverse-sorted insertion order → guaranteed worst-case skewed tree.

name: Search-Path / Probe-Sequence Validity
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek target key search kiya ja raha hai BST me, aur ek CANDIDATE sequence of examined nodes di hai — poocha hai ye sequence POSSIBLE hai ya nahi (valid search path) — ye validity-check pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: A valid search path must progressively NARROW the range [low,high) toward the target — each new node's value must lie strictly within the range established by all PREVIOUS nodes in the path relative to the target.
If any candidate value falls outside the currently-narrowed valid range, the sequence is IMPOSSIBLE.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. For each node in the candidate sequence: check it's within the current range AND on the correct side of the target to be a legitimate 'next step' toward it.
3. Update the range based on whether this node is greater or less than the target (narrowing from that side).
4. If any step violates the range, the sequence is INVALID.
variationsObserved: 'How many different valid orderings are possible' for a search path — combinatorial counting variant, not just single-sequence validity.
Failed/unsuccessful search (target not in tree) — same range-narrowing logic applies up to the point of failure.
commonTraps: Only checking pairwise consecutive-node ordering instead of the full cumulative range constraint.

name: BST-Specific Traversal Properties (preorder→postorder, sorted-inorder checks)
recognitionClueHinglish: Preorder ya postorder traversal di hai (BST guarantee ke saath) aur poocha hai DUSRA traversal kya hoga, ya diye gaye sequences me se kaunse VALID inorder/preorder sequences ho sakte hain BST ke — ye is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (36 me se 8 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Inorder of ANY BST = sorted order — instant check for 'is this a valid inorder sequence'.

Preorder→Postorder conversion WITHOUT building the full tree: root=first element of preorder; partition REST into <root (left subtree preorder) and >root (right subtree preorder); recurse; assemble postorder as (left-postorder)+(right-postorder)+(root).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For 'is this a valid inorder' questions: just check if the sequence is sorted.
2. For preorder→postorder (or similar) conversion: use the partition-by-value recursive technique — much faster than drawing the whole tree.
3. Double check by building the actual tree if the partition gets confusing with duplicate-looking values.
variationsObserved: Postorder given, inorder asked (same partition trick works, using postorder's LAST element as root instead of preorder's first).
commonTraps: Trying to reconstruct the full tree via general (non-BST) methods needing inorder+preorder together — the BST-specific shortcut needs only ONE traversal plus the ordering property.

name: Counting Distinct BSTs (Catalan number application)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai 'how many distinct BSTs can be formed with n distinct keys' — ye direct Catalan-number-recall pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Number of distinct BSTs with n distinct keys = Catalan number C(n) = (2n)!/((n+1)!n!) — SAME formula as counting unlabeled binary tree shapes, since each shape has exactly ONE valid BST-key-assignment.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Recall or derive C(n) = Σ(i=0 to n-1) C(i)·C(n-1-i) [choosing each possible root, recursively counting left/right BST shapes], or just plug into the closed form (2n)!/((n+1)!n!).
2. For small n, it's often faster to compute C(n) directly from the recurrence than the factorial formula.
commonTraps: Confusing this with 2^n or n! — it's specifically the Catalan number, a distinct and slower-growing sequence than n! but faster than a simple exponential for small n.

name: BST Operation Complexity (search/insert/delete/range-query, balanced vs skewed)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai search/insert/delete/range-query ki worst-case time complexity kya hai for a BST (ya specifically ek BALANCED BST) — ye is topic ka doosra sabse bada pattern hai (36 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: ALWAYS check: is the tree stated to be BALANCED? If yes → O(log n). If not specified or explicitly skewed-possible → worst case O(n) (or O(h) generally).
Range query reporting k elements: O(h+k) for a balanced tree — the h to locate the range, k to walk through and report results.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Check explicitly whether 'balanced' is stated in the problem.
2. If balanced: apply O(log n) for search/insert/delete, O(log n + k) for range queries reporting k elements.
3. If NOT guaranteed balanced: worst case is O(n) (fully skewed tree scenario) — pick this unless the question specifically asks for average/expected case.
variationsObserved: Multi-operation combined systems (min-extraction + insertion + a custom operation, asked for overall complexity) — analyze each operation type separately then combine.
Minimum/maximum possible HEIGHT for n nodes (not operation complexity per se, but the height bound that DRIVES complexity) — Min height ≈ ⌊log2 n⌋, Max height = n-1 (skewed).
commonTraps: Defaulting to O(log n) without checking if the BALANCED assumption actually holds in the specific question.
